title: Dividing in a clock: modular inverses
summary: ECDSA, RSA, and Diffie–Hellman all need division modulo a prime. Fermat's little theorem turns that into an exponentiation. We compute a⁻¹ mod p on numbers small enough to check by hand.

case.name: ECDSA / RFC 6979 dependence on modular inversion
case.impact: Signature and key-agreement formulas are undefined without a⁻¹ mod n; bugs and leaked partial inverses have repeatedly turned into private-key recovery

body:
In ordinary arithmetic, dividing by a means multiplying by 1/a. In modular arithmetic mod p you need an integer a⁻¹ such that
  a · a⁻¹ ≡ 1 (mod p).
That integer exists if and only if gcd(a, p) = 1. When p is prime and a ≢ 0 (mod p), every nonzero residue has a unique inverse in 1…p−1.

Fermat's little theorem supplies a formula. For prime p and a not divisible by p,
  a^{p−1} ≡ 1 (mod p),
hence a · a^{p−2} ≡ 1 (mod p), so
  a⁻¹ ≡ a^{p−2} (mod p).
You can evaluate that with fast exponentiation (square-and-multiply). The extended Euclidean algorithm gives the same inverse and often runs faster; both are correct. What matters for security reviews is that the inverse is well-defined and that implementations do not leak it through timing — modular inversion has historically been a side-channel favorite next to modular exponentiation.

Where the inverse shows up in systems you already study: ECDSA's s = k⁻¹(z + r·d) mod n needs k⁻¹; recovering k from nonce reuse (see the PS3 lesson) is exactly rearranging that formula. Diffie–Hellman and ECDH treat exponentiation in a prime-order group where every nonzero scalar is invertible. RSA's decryption exponent d is defined as the inverse of e modulo φ(n) (or λ(n)). If e and φ(n) are not coprime, the keygen is broken before you start.

Worked example: p = 101, a = 17. Compute 17^{99} mod 101, or run extended Euclid on (17, 101). Either way a⁻¹ ≡ 6 (mod 101), because 17·6 = 102 ≡ 1 (mod 101). Always multiply back to verify: one check catches arithmetic mistakes that would poison a longer CTF solve.

Red flags in code: inversion without a gcd/coprimality check on composite moduli; using Fermat with a composite modulus (the formula can fail); and constant-time claims that still call a variable-time invert routine. For hand solves, prefer Fermat when the modulus is a small prime and you have a pow(base, exp, mod) tool, and prefer extended Euclid when you want the Bézout coefficients too.

exercise.statement: Let p = 101 (prime) and a = 17. Compute a⁻¹ mod p using Fermat: a^{p−2} mod p. Answer ZKCTF{inv} with the representative in 1…100.
artifacts:
p = 101
a = 17
inv = pow(a, p-2, p)   # or extended Euclid
Check: (a * inv) % p == 1
hints: The inverse is a single digit; verify by multiplying back by 17.
